1. Neonatal Jaundice Basics and Bilirubin Metabolism

  • Gestational age is an important predictor of jaundice, mainly because of hepatic enzyme maturation.
  • Up to 84% of term infants develop jaundice; post-term jaundice is very rare; up to 80% of preterm infants; nearly all low and very low birthweight infants.

Bilirubin metabolism (10 steps on the slide)

  1. Senescent red cells are the major source of heme proteins; the more RBC breakdown, the more bilirubin.
  2. Heme → bilirubin in macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system (tissue macrophages, spleen, liver).
  3. Unconjugated bilirubin travels in blood bound to albumin to the liver.
  4. Taken up by facilitated diffusion and conjugated with glucuronic acid (UDP-glucuronyl transferase).
  5. Conjugated bilirubin is actively secreted into bile, then the intestine.
  6. In the intestine, bacteria remove glucuronic acid and convert bilirubin to urobilinogen.
  7. Some urobilinogen is reabsorbed into portal blood (enterohepatic cycle).
  8. Part re-enters the enterohepatic urobilinogen cycle.
  9. The rest goes to the kidney and becomes urobilin (yellow urine).
  10. Urobilinogen is oxidized by gut bacteria to brown stercobilin (stool).
Bilirubin metabolism (slide 4) (click to enlarge)
What controls bilirubin level(1) Amount of RBC breakdown, (2) liver conjugation capacity (UDP-glucuronyl transferase), (3) albumin to carry unconjugated bilirubin, (4) excretion and enterohepatic recirculation.

Why newborns are jaundiced (mechanism slide)

PhysiologicNonphysiologic (pathologic)
Catabolism of heme from fetal erythrocyte breakdown (and myoglobin, cytochromes, catalase)Increased heme catabolism: congenital hemolytic anemias (G6PD, spherocytosis), immune hemolysis (Rh, ABO), extravasated blood (bruising, fractures, intracranial hemorrhage)
Decreased uptake and excretion: low ligandin (intracellular binding protein), low UDPGT activityDecreased conjugation and excretion: genetic UGT defects (Crigler-Najjar, Gilbert); hepatic and biliary disease (neonatal hepatitis, biliary atresia)
Low albuminIncreased enterohepatic circulation: decreased bowel passage (intestinal atresia, NEC, fasting, inadequate nutrition = "breastfeeding jaundice") or increased deconjugation in bowel (breast milk jaundice)

2. Risk Factors, Causes and Differential Diagnosis

Risk factors for significant hyperbilirubinemia

  • Lower gestational age (risk rises with each week below 40).
  • Jaundice in the first 24 hours (jaundice usually appears after 24 h; early jaundice suggests something significant).
  • Predischarge TcB or TSB close to the phototherapy threshold.
  • Hemolysis from any cause, suspected by a rapid rise in TSB/TcB: >0.3 mg/dL per hour in the first 24 h or >0.2 mg/dL per hour thereafter.
  • Phototherapy before discharge; parent or sibling needing phototherapy or exchange transfusion.
  • Family history or ancestry suggesting inherited RBC disorders (G6PD).
  • Exclusive breastfeeding with suboptimal intake; scalp hematoma or significant bruising; Down syndrome; macrosomic infant of a diabetic mother.

Direct bilirubin comes from two major causes: bile flow obstruction or hepatocellular injury.

3. Physiologic vs Pathologic Jaundice, Breastfeeding vs Breast Milk

PhysiologicPathologic
MechanismImmature bilirubin elimination and increased production; shortened RBC lifespan and immature liver enzymesJaundice requiring treatment: hemolysis, sepsis, extravascular blood, polycythemia, abnormal enterohepatic circulation, anatomic liver abnormalities, endocrine/metabolic disorders
Bilirubin typeUnconjugated (indirect)Unconjugated or conjugated
TimingRises after the first day; levels off at 3-5 daysWithin the first 24 hours, or prolonged >2 weeks
LevelsCommon; usually needs only nutritional support, occasionally phototherapyTotal bilirubin >12-15 mg/dL in an otherwise healthy term infant
Direct bilirubin—Conjugated ≥1.0 mg/dL or >15% of total = pathologic; ≥5 mg/dL likely cholestatic (e.g. biliary atresia)
Risk—Severe hyperbilirubinemia and kernicterus
  • Breastfed infants have a 3-6 fold higher risk of higher bilirubin levels, and a third may have physiologic jaundice persisting beyond 2 weeks. Almost no post-term infants develop physiologic jaundice.
  • Visual assessment (cephalocaudal progression) is inaccurate because of differences in color perception; sclera and under the tongue help, especially in infants of color, but use TcB/TSB for decisions.

Breastfeeding vs breast milk jaundice

Breastfeeding jaundiceBreast milk jaundice
TimingEarly; peaks day 3-5Starts in the first week; persists beyond 2 weeks
CauseMild dehydration and excessive weight loss (poor latch/low intake); ↓ urine and stool output so bilirubin is retained (↑ enterohepatic circulation)Bilirubin stays high despite adequate volume and weight gain; breast milk is thought to slow bilirubin metabolism at glucuronyl transferase (↑ deconjugation)
BabyNot feeding well, dehydratedFeeding well, growing, good urine/stool output
ManagementLactation consultant early; feed at least 8 times/day; supplement with donor milk or formula if neededNo specific measures on his slide; evaluate as for any prolonged jaundice (>2 weeks is a pathologic criterion)

4. Hemolytic Causes: G6PD, Rh(D) and ABO Incompatibility

HemolyticNon-hemolytic
Immune: ABO and Rh(D)
Non-immune enzymatic: G6PD, pyruvate kinase deficiency
RBC membrane: spherocytosis, elliptocytosis (also sickle cell in his narration)		Polycythemia
Bruising / internal bleeding: cephalohematoma, subgaleal hemorrhage
Breastfeeding / breast milk jaundice
Glucuronyl transferase: Gilbert, Crigler-Najjar
Hypothyroidism, hypoalbuminemia, ↑ enterohepatic circulation
  • Why is polycythemia non-hemolytic? Nothing abnormal is destroying cells; the normal breakdown of an excess of RBCs produces more bilirubin.
  • G6PD deficiency (his narration): G6PD protects RBCs from oxidative substances; X-linked; more common where malaria is endemic (Mediterranean, Southeast Asian, African populations; ~13% of African American males).

Rh(D) incompatibility

  • Mother is Rh negative, fetus Rh positive. Maternal exposure to fetal blood → anti-Rh(D) antibodies that cross the placenta, attach to fetal RBCs and cause hemolysis.
  • Usually in the second and subsequent pregnancies (time to make antibodies after the first).
  • Fetal-to-maternal exposure: birth, miscarriage, amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling, external cephalic version, blunt trauma, ectopic pregnancy.
  • Prophylaxis: RhoGAM at 28 weeks and at delivery (if baby is Rh+), and with any of the exposures above.

ABO incompatibility

  • Occurs in ~15% of pregnancies; only ~4% of newborns have hemolytic disease.
  • Mother type O makes IgG that crosses the placenta; baby type A, B or AB is affected. Mothers A, B or AB make IgM, which cannot cross.
  • Peak immune hemolysis in the first week; maternal antibodies can persist up to 6 weeks.
  • Milder than Rh disease and does not require RhoGAM-type immune globulin prophylaxis.
Rh(D)ABO
Mother / babyRh negative / Rh positiveType O / type A, B or AB
AntibodyIgG anti-DIgG (from type O mothers)
SeverityMore severeMilder
PreventionRhoGAMNone (no immune globulin)
Management of anti-erythrocyte antibodies (flowchart)All newborns: was the maternal antibody screen done and is it positive? If not done or positive → infant DAT and blood type as soon as possible. If infant DAT is negative → return to routine guidelines. If DAT positive and ALL true (DAT positive only for anti-Rh(D), mother received RhIG in pregnancy, mother not known to be anti-D positive before RhIG) → routine guidelines. Otherwise treat as having a neurotoxicity risk factor: measure TcB/TSB immediately, then every 4 h x2, then every 12 h x3, and follow therapy charts. (His narration: ~30% false-negative DAT, so watch closely.)

5. Kernicterus and Neurotoxicity Risk Factors

  • Kernicterus = irreversible bilirubin encephalopathy; about 1 in 100,000 infants.
  • Symptoms: lethargy, hypotonia (early) then hypertonia, athetosis, back and neck arching (opisthotonus/retrocollis), irritability, high-pitched cry (apnea in severe).

Hyperbilirubinemia neurotoxicity risk factors (listed in order of importance)

  • Gestational age <38 weeks (risk rises with prematurity)
  • Hemolytic disease of the newborn (positive DAT with ABO, Rh(D) or minor antigen incompatibility)
  • G6PD deficiency
  • Other hemolytic conditions: pyruvate kinase deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis
  • Albumin <3 g/dL
  • Sepsis
  • Asphyxia
  • Clinical instability in the past 24 hours
  • Acidosis
Neurotoxicity risk factors (slide 15) (click to enlarge)
Why these matter(Standard physiology, not on his slide: low albumin and acidosis raise free bilirubin, which can enter the brain.) Neurotoxicity risk factors lower the phototherapy and exchange thresholds (use the "one or more risk factors" charts).

6. Screening, Phototherapy and Lab Work

Transcutaneous bilirubin meter (TcB)

  • Screens which baby needs a serum level, reducing blood draws.
  • Accuracy: ±3 mg/dL of the serum value (a TcB of 9 could be 6 or 12).
  • Not accurate above 15 mg/dL.
  • Get a TSB if the TcB is within 3 mg/dL of the phototherapy threshold, above it, or ≥15 mg/dL. Use total serum bilirubin (do not subtract direct bilirubin).

Phototherapy

  • First-line treatment for hyperbilirubinemia that meets criteria.
  • Converts bilirubin to a water-soluble isomer cleared in urine or stool. (His narration: blue light ~475 nm; sunlight is not recommended because of sunburn and full-spectrum exposure.)
  • Started using the chart by hours of age, gestational age, bilirubin level and presence of neurotoxicity risk factors.
  • Breastfeeding may continue (take baby out of the light to feed).
  • Stop when bilirubin is >2 mg/dL below the phototherapy threshold (wait longer if extra risk factors).
  • Recheck TSB 12-24 h after stopping, or 6-12 h if hemolytic cause; after 24 h may use TcB.
Phototherapy thresholds, no neurotoxicity risk factors (slide 22) (click to enlarge)
Phototherapy thresholds, 1 or more neurotoxicity risk factors (slide 23) (click to enlarge)
Risks of phototherapy
Short termTemperature instability, diarrhea (watch dehydration), physical separation from parents, prolonged hospitalization
Long termIncreased seizure risk in males (2-7 per 1000); conflicting evidence of cancer risk (~1 per 1000: leukemia, renal, hepatic)

Lab work

If therapy is needed before 48 hours of ageOngoing
CBC, DAT (direct Coombs), G6PD concentration, end-tidal COTSB within 12 h of starting phototherapy; every 4-6 h if suspected hemolysis or neurotoxicity risk factors
  • End-tidal CO (his narration): heme catabolism produces equimolar CO and bilirubin, so ETCO is an index of hemolysis and bilirubin production.

Home phototherapy: ALL must be met

  • Gestational age ≥38 weeks; ≥48 hours old; clinically well with adequate feeding.
  • No neurotoxicity risk factors; no previous phototherapy.
  • TSB no more than 1 mg/dL above the phototherapy threshold.
  • LED device available at home without delay; TSB can be measured daily.

7. Escalation of Care and Exchange Transfusion

  • Escalate when TSB is within 2 mg/dL of the exchange transfusion threshold (<2 mg/dL below it) or above it.
  • Use the exchange thresholds with or without neurotoxicity risk factors; thresholds are lower when risk factors are present.
  • Baby must be in a NICU where exchange transfusion is done; transfer if not.
  • STAT labs: total and direct bilirubin, CBC, albumin, chemistry panel, type and cross; TSB every 2 hours.
  • While preparing: intensive phototherapy, IV hydration, notify the blood bank (blood takes time to prepare, up to ~4 h); IVIG if DAT positive.
  • If TSB falls below the escalation level during preparation, return to regular phototherapy and monitor; if still elevated, continue intensive therapy and be ready to exchange.
Exchange transfusion thresholds, no risk factors (slide 27) (click to enlarge)
Exchange transfusion thresholds, 1 or more risk factors (slide 28) (click to enlarge)

Exchange transfusion

  • Indications: meets threshold on the graph, or signs of bilirubin encephalopathy with bilirubin near the threshold: hypertonia, retrocollis, arching, high-pitched cry, apnea, opisthotonus.
  • Process: exchange 160 mL/kg of the baby's blood (2-15 mL at a time) with RBCs plus fresh frozen plasma to an Hct of 40-45 (FFP supplies albumin to bind bilirubin).
  • If bilirubin decreases while waiting for blood, hold the transfusion and keep monitoring.
StepIntervention
Meets phototherapy thresholdPhototherapy
TSB <2 mg/dL below exchange thresholdEscalate: NICU, STAT labs, TSB q2h, intensive phototherapy, IV fluids, IVIG if DAT+
At or above exchange threshold, or encephalopathy signsExchange transfusion

8. Discharge Criteria, Prevention and a Worked Case

Discharge algorithm (infant ≥12 h old, not treated)

  • Determine the hour-specific phototherapy threshold (gestational age + neurotoxicity risk). If TSB is at or above it → begin phototherapy.
  • Otherwise use phototherapy threshold minus TcB/TSB to decide follow-up:
Threshold minus TcB/TSBRecommendation
0.1-1.9 mg/dL<24 h old: delay discharge, consider phototherapy, TSB in 4-8 h. ≥24 h: TSB in 4-24 h; options: delay discharge, home phototherapy if criteria met, or discharge with close follow-up
2.0-3.4TSB or TcB in 4-24 h
3.5-5.4TSB or TcB in 1-2 days
5.5-6.9Discharging <72 h: follow-up within 2 days; ≥72 h: clinical judgment
≥7.0Discharging <72 h: follow-up within 3 days; ≥72 h: clinical judgment
Hospital discharge criteria (slide 30) (click to enlarge)

Examples from the lecture: threshold 12, TcB 11 (difference 1) → first row (delay discharge, recheck soon). Threshold 15, TSB 6 (difference 9) → last row (follow-up within 3 days if discharged <72 h).

Prevention

  • Prevent isoimmune hemolytic disease: test the mother for blood type and Rh(D); give RhoGAM if Rh(D) negative at 28 weeks (or earlier if risk of fetal blood crossing: trauma, miscarriage, prior untreated delivery) and after delivery of an Rh(D)+ infant.
  • Test the infant at birth with a DAT if the maternal antibody screen is positive or unknown (not screened).
  • Provide feeding support (hydration, adequate intake).

Worked case from the lecture

  • 39-week breastfed newborn, 48 hours old, no neurotoxicity risk factors; TcB is high (>15 mg/dL, so inaccurate).
  • Get a TSB: 18 mg/dL. The no-risk-factor phototherapy threshold for a 39-week infant at 48 h is about 17 (chart), so start phototherapy and recheck TSB (within 12 h per his lab slide).
  • If the same baby had one neurotoxicity risk factor, the threshold falls markedly (about 14 at 48 h), so an 18 is even further above it.
